The platform team needs one consistent way to view, access and configure every cluster, including those outside Google Cloud, without giving cluster API servers public IP addresses. What should the architect propose?

choices.text: Convert every cluster to Autopilot so that Google manages the clusters sitting in the colocation facility
choices.rationale: Autopilot is a GKE mode on Google Cloud. It does not take over clusters running in a colocation facility.

choices.text: Give each colocation cluster's API server a public IP and manage them all with separate kubectl contexts
choices.rationale: This breaks the no-public-IP requirement and keeps management fragmented, with a different context and configuration per cluster.

choices.text: Register all clusters in a fleet, attach external ones with the Connect Agent, and use Connect gateway and fleet config
choices.rationale: Fleets group clusters across projects and environments. The Connect Agent works through NATs and VPNs, so API servers need no public IPs, and Connect gateway gives consistent access.

choices.text: Run one large Standard cluster on Google Cloud and move every colocation workload into it immediately
choices.rationale: The stem says the colocation clusters must remain for years because of the legacy integrations, so an immediate consolidation is not an option.

prompt: A Cloud Run API on default autoscaling opens a small connection pool per instance to a Cloud SQL instance that allows 500 connections. Launch-day spikes scale the service to many instances and the database starts refusing connections. The team wants to protect the database while still serving as much traffic as it can handle. What should they do?

choices.text: Raise minimum instances to the expected peak, so that no scale-out happens during the launch-day spike
choices.rationale: Pre-provisioning peak capacity still opens a pool per instance, can exceed the database limit anyway, and bills for idle instances.

choices.text: Set a service-level maximum instances value so that instances times pool size stays under the connection limit
choices.rationale: Maximum instances is the documented control for limiting connections to a backing service such as a database. A service-level value takes effect immediately.

choices.text: Configure the service to scale on memory utilization so that instances are added only when containers come under memory pressure
choices.rationale: Cloud Run does not support scaling on memory utilization. Its autoscaler uses CPU utilization and request concurrency.

choices.text: Raise the revision's maximum instances so traffic can spread across more containers with smaller pools
choices.rationale: More instances means more pools and more connections, which makes the exhaustion worse.

prompt: A single-threaded Python image-rendering service runs on Cloud Run with 4 vCPUs per instance and maximum concurrent requests set to 80. In load tests, p99 latency passes 9 seconds while average CPU utilization stays near 25% and the autoscaler holds at three instances. What is the best change?

choices.text: Raise maximum concurrency to 1,000 so that each instance absorbs far more of the incoming request load
choices.rationale: More concurrent requests per single-threaded instance deepens the queue on the one busy thread and raises latency further.

choices.text: Increase CPUs per instance to 8 so the rendering process has more CPU headroom while it handles requests
choices.rationale: A single thread cannot use extra cores, and a larger instance lowers average utilization even more, which keeps CPU-based scaling from firing.

choices.text: Set minimum instances to 10 so cold starts disappear and spare capacity is always warm and ready for new requests
choices.rationale: Latency here comes from queuing on busy threads, not cold starts. Ten always-on 4-vCPU instances only add cost while the scaling signal stays wrong.

choices.text: Cut CPUs per instance to fit the single thread and lower maximum concurrency so request load drives scale-out
choices.rationale: One busy thread on 4 vCPUs reads as about 25% average CPU, below the 60% target, so CPU scaling never triggers. Lower concurrency lets request throughput add instances.

prompt: Altostrat's transcoding runs in an event-driven Cloud Run function triggered when a file lands in Cloud Storage. Feature-length documentaries take up to three hours to transcode, and the function is cut off long before that. The team wants to keep the event-driven trigger, avoid managing servers and process many files in parallel. What should they change?

choices.text: Raise the event-driven function's timeout to three hours in its second-generation configuration settings
choices.rationale: Event-driven functions are limited to 9 minutes, so a three-hour value cannot be configured.

choices.text: Rewrite the transcoder as a Cloud Run service that the function calls and then waits on synchronously for each file
choices.rationale: A Cloud Run service request timeout can be raised to at most 60 minutes, so a three-hour request would still be cut off.

choices.text: Keep the function as a trigger that starts a Cloud Run job execution per file, with task timeouts up to 168 hours
choices.rationale: Jobs run to completion, allow task timeouts up to 7 days and support many parallel tasks. The function stays as a lightweight, event-driven launcher.

choices.text: Switch the function to an HTTP function and raise its timeout to the 60-minute maximum that it allows
choices.rationale: HTTP functions top out at 60 minutes, which is still shorter than a three-hour transcode.

explanation: Cloud Run functions (2nd gen) allow 540 seconds for event-driven and 60 minutes for HTTP functions (functions/quotas). Cloud Run service requests top out at 60 minutes, while Cloud Run jobs allow task timeouts up to 168 hours (run/docs/create-jobs).

prompt: KnightMotives runs a nightly regression of its autonomous-driving simulator: about 5,000 independent scenarios of 15 to 40 minutes each, sharing no state. Failed scenarios can simply be rerun. The team does not want to operate a scheduler or cluster and wants the lowest compute cost. Which design fits best?

choices.text: A GKE Autopilot cluster running a hand-built queue consumer that pulls scenarios from Pub/Sub
choices.rationale: This means writing and operating a scheduler and a queue, and it pays regular per-Pod rates rather than Spot discounts.

choices.text: On-demand Compute Engine VMs that each pull scenarios from a Pub/Sub topic through a startup script
choices.rationale: It works but needs custom orchestration, retry logic and cleanup, and it uses the most expensive provisioning model.

choices.text: A stateful MIG of on-demand VMs that a Cloud Scheduler script resizes each evening and each morning
choices.rationale: A stateful MIG is built for per-VM identity, not stateless fan-out. It also leaves custom scheduling and on-demand pricing in place.

choices.text: A Batch job with one task per scenario, capped parallelism, Spot provisioning and a small retry count
choices.rationale: Batch provisions and tears down the VMs itself. SPOT provisioning cuts cost for restartable work, taskCount and parallelism fit independent scenarios, and maxRetryCount (0 to 10) reruns failures.

prompt: A company brings a database engine licensed per physical core to Compute Engine. The workload must stay highly available through host maintenance by using live migration, and auditors require a report of the physical cores consumed. Which two actions meet these needs? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Run on multi-tenant hosts under License Mobility, since per-core licenses never need dedicated hardware
choices.rationale: License Mobility applies to Microsoft applications. Licenses tied to physical cores generally require compliant dedicated hardware such as sole-tenant nodes.

choices.text: Enable the Cloud Logging API and analyze sole-tenant node usage data in BigQuery for physical core counts
choices.rationale: Logging data on node usage can be queried in BigQuery to report physical cores, which is the tracking Google recommends for per-core licenses.

choices.text: Create a node group with the migrate-within-node-group maintenance policy and reserve the holdback capacity it needs
choices.rationale: This policy live migrates VMs within a fixed set of physical servers, which limits the unique servers (and cores) used. Compute Engine reserves holdback nodes (1 per 20) for the migrations.

choices.text: Use restart-in-place, which keeps VMs on one server and live migrates them so availability is unaffected
choices.rationale: Restart-in-place stops VMs during host events and restarts them on the same server. That means downtime of up to about an hour and no live migration.

choices.text: Keep the Default maintenance policy, because VMs then live migrate only among a fixed set of physical servers
choices.rationale: The Default policy lets VMs migrate to any server in the group, so it is not suitable when physical core usage must be minimized.

prompt: An enterprise is sizing Google Cloud VMware Engine private clouds for a lift-and-shift of vSphere workloads, some of which carry per-core licensing. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)

choices.text: The customer must patch ESXi hosts and replace failed bare-metal hardware in the private cloud
choices.rationale: Google manages the infrastructure layer of the VMware stack. Customers manage workloads through vCenter and NSX Manager.

choices.text: A standard private cloud needs at least three nodes per cluster and is the configuration that qualifies for the SLA
choices.rationale: Standard private clouds require a minimum of three nodes per cluster and are SLA-eligible. Single-node private clouds are not.

choices.text: Autoscale policies add and remove nodes in single-node private clouds as demand rises and falls
choices.rationale: Autoscaling is not available for single-node private clouds. Expanding to three or more nodes is the upgrade path.

choices.text: A single-node private cloud suits production because vSphere HA restarts its VMs on a spare host if one fails
choices.rationale: Single-node clouds have no vSphere HA or DRS, use FTT=0 storage that risks data loss, and are meant for proof of concept and testing.

choices.text: Custom core counts can lower the enabled cores per node to meet licensing limits without changing node pricing
choices.rationale: The service lets you reduce the cores available per node for licensing reasons, and the price of the node stays the same.

prompt: A containerized data-cleanup program runs for about 40 minutes each night, writes its results to Cloud Storage and then exits. It never listens for HTTP requests. The team wants a serverless option with no cluster to run. Which fits best?

choices.text: An App Engine flexible environment service
choices.rationale: Flexible keeps at least one instance running at all times and is meant for request-serving apps, not a nightly run-to-completion task.

choices.text: A Cloud Run job that a scheduler triggers each night
choices.rationale: Jobs execute tasks to completion and exit, with a default task timeout of 10 minutes that can be raised to 7 days. They suit scheduled batch work that serves no requests.

choices.text: A Cloud Run service with minimum instances set to 1
choices.rationale: A service is built to listen for requests. Holding an instance idle just to run a nightly program wastes money and fits the model poorly.

choices.text: An event-driven Cloud Run function started on a timer
choices.rationale: Event-driven functions are limited to 9 minutes, so a 40-minute run would be cut off.

prompt: A production GKE Standard cluster was created as a zonal cluster. During a zone outage the team could not reach the Kubernetes API, and they also see API unavailability during control plane upgrades. Which cluster type avoids both problems for new production clusters?

choices.text: A regional cluster, replicating the control plane across zones
choices.rationale: Regional clusters keep the API available through a zone failure and during control plane upgrades or resizes, and distribute nodes across zones by default.

choices.text: Two zonal clusters in the same zone, fronted by an internal load balancer
choices.rationale: Both control planes share the failure domain of that one zone, so a zone outage still removes API access.

choices.text: A zonal cluster with extra node pools placed in two more zones
choices.rationale: Extra node zones spread workloads, but the control plane still runs in one zone and remains a single point of failure.

choices.text: A zonal cluster with the cluster autoscaler enabled on every pool
choices.rationale: The autoscaler resizes node pools. It does nothing for control plane availability.

prompt: A retailer scores 40 million customer records every Sunday with a trained churn model on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Inputs live in BigQuery, results go back to BigQuery and nobody needs a prediction in real time. Which serving approach fits best?

choices.text: Deploy the model to an online endpoint and call it once per record from a script
choices.rationale: Online inference is for low-latency, per-request predictions. Forty million individual calls add cost and complexity for a weekly job.

choices.text: Run the predictions interactively from a notebook cell each Sunday
choices.rationale: A manual notebook run is not repeatable or scalable, and it lacks the managed throughput and BigQuery integration of a batch job.

choices.text: A batch inference job that reads from BigQuery and needs no deployed endpoint
choices.rationale: Batch inference processes large datasets asynchronously, accepts BigQuery or Cloud Storage input and avoids endpoint management entirely.

choices.text: Keep an online endpoint with a high minimum replica count so the weekly run finishes fast
choices.rationale: Paying for replicas around the clock to serve one weekly burst is wasteful, and the job still needs a request loop.

prompt: A fraud model is served from an Agent Platform endpoint that mobile clients call at a fixed endpoint URL. The team has a retrained model and wants to send 10% of live traffic to it, compare outcomes and raise its share gradually without any client change. What should they do?

choices.text: Deploy the new model to the same endpoint with a 10% traffic split, then raise the share gradually
choices.rationale: An endpoint can serve several deployed models with a configurable traffic split, so the URL stays the same and the new model takes more traffic step by step.

choices.text: Create a second endpoint and ask the clients to alternate between the two endpoint URLs
choices.rationale: That forces a client change and splits traffic in application code rather than in the endpoint.

choices.text: Undeploy the current model, deploy the new one, and roll back only if complaints arrive
choices.rationale: This switches 100% of traffic at once, with downtime risk, and gives no gradual comparison.

choices.text: Deploy the new model to a separate endpoint and repoint DNS to it once the first smoke tests have passed
choices.rationale: A DNS cutover is all-or-nothing and does not provide a controlled 10% sample of live traffic.

prompt: A team manages several versions of a recommendation model in the Agent Platform Model Registry and wants deployments to reference versions by name instead of by version ID. Which two statements about model version aliases are accurate? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Every model keeps exactly one default alias, and that version is used when no version is named
choices.rationale: The first version receives the default alias, one version must carry it at all times, and commands that omit a version use it.

choices.text: Alias names must be numeric so that they can be told apart from labels and from model names
choices.rationale: Aliases must be non-numerical and match a specific pattern, which is what distinguishes them from version IDs.

choices.text: Moving a custom alias such as production to another version lets deployments reference the model by name
choices.rationale: An alias is a mutable, named reference, similar to a Docker tag or Git branch, and can be moved from one version to another.

choices.text: One alias can point at several versions of the same model, so staging and production can share it
choices.rationale: An alias can be assigned to only one version per model at a time. Assigning it again removes it from the earlier version.

choices.text: Aliases and labels are interchangeable, so a label filter can select the version to deploy
choices.rationale: An alias is different from a label. Labels are metadata, while aliases are named pointers to a version.

prompt: The ranker-prod endpoint serves a GPU-backed model, with CPU-heavy tokenization and image decoding inside the serving container. Replicas climbed to the configured maximum during a sustained traffic rise, latency stayed flat and the bill jumped. No autoscaling metric is configured. Which change addresses the root cause?

exhibit.label: ranker-prod deployment and metrics
exhibit.content:
machine: a2-highgpu-1g (1 GPU)   minReplicaCount=2  maxReplicaCount=8   autoscalingMetricSpecs: (not set)

time   replicas  cpu_util  gpu_duty_cycle  p95_latency_ms  req/min/replica
10:00  2         52%       31%             48              900
10:20  4         74%       29%             46              880
10:40  8         78%       27%             47              850
11:00  8         81%       26%             49              840

choices.text: Raise maxReplicaCount so that the endpoint can keep adding replicas until CPU usage falls below 60%
choices.rationale: That lets the cost climb further. The default rule keeps adding GPU replicas for a CPU-bound step while GPU duty cycle stays near 26 to 31%.

choices.text: Set minimum replicas to 0 so that the endpoint releases all of its replicas whenever traffic is quiet
choices.rationale: Scale to zero is a Preview feature, and it does not change which signal drives scale-out when traffic returns.

choices.text: Move the model to batch inference, which scales its replicas automatically as the load changes
choices.rationale: Batch inference nodes do not autoscale (they use a starting replica count), and the workload still needs real-time answers.

choices.text: Set autoscalingMetricSpecs to scale on GPU duty cycle or request count instead of the default rule
choices.rationale: By default the endpoint scales to keep the higher of CPU and GPU usage near 60%. Here CPU preprocessing is the higher number, so replicas grow while the GPUs sit mostly idle.

prompt: A nightly retraining pipeline on Agent Platform Pipelines keeps reporting an unchanged model even though the source table is rebuilt every night. The team wants expensive steps skipped only when their inputs truly have not changed. Based on the run log in the exhibit, what is the best fix?

exhibit.label: Pipeline run log (pipeline name: churn-nightly)
exhibit.content:
2026-09-28  extract-features  inputs={sql: 'SELECT * FROM mart.features_latest'}  EXECUTED  34m12s
2026-09-29  extract-features  inputs={sql: 'SELECT * FROM mart.features_latest'}  CACHED    0s
2026-09-30  extract-features  inputs={sql: 'SELECT * FROM mart.features_latest'}  CACHED    0s
2026-09-30  train-model       inputs={features: artifact b41}                     CACHED    0s
note: mart.features_latest rebuilt nightly; AUC identical to 4 decimals since 2026-09-28

choices.text: Turn off caching for the whole pipeline job so every step reruns every night
choices.rationale: This fixes staleness but also reruns steps whose inputs have not changed, which defeats the cost goal.

choices.text: Delete the compiled pipeline template and compile it again, which clears the execution cache
choices.rationale: The cache lives in the ML metadata store and is keyed on step inputs and component specs. Recompiling the template does not clear it.

choices.text: Pass the run date or a snapshot ID into the extract step, or turn caching off for that task alone
choices.rationale: A step is skipped when its inputs and component spec match an earlier execution. The constant SQL string makes the cache key identical every night, so changing the input (or disabling caching for that task) fixes it while later steps still cache.

choices.text: Retrain with a deeper model, because identical AUC across runs means the current model is underfitting
choices.rationale: The identical metric is a symptom of reused cached outputs, not model capacity. The training step never saw new data.

choices.text: Wait for the cached result to expire, since execution cache entries have a 24-hour time to live
choices.rationale: Cached results have no time to live. They remain reusable until the entry is deleted from the metadata store.

prompt: A research team trains a model with a custom training job on four A2 nodes with one A100 each. All nodes must start together, the job runs about 36 hours and has no hard start time. On-demand requests keep failing for lack of GPU capacity, and Spot VMs are ruled out because a preemption would waste progress. What should they configure?

choices.text: Set the job's scheduling strategy to FLEX_START with a maximum wait so it starts when every GPU is available
choices.rationale: Dynamic Workload Scheduler (flex-start) queues GPU jobs until the requested resources are available, which suits multi-node jobs that cannot start until all nodes are ready.

choices.text: Request a larger on-demand GPU quota, since a quota increase reserves physical capacity in the region for you
choices.rationale: Quota is a permission ceiling, not reserved hardware. A bigger quota does not create capacity when the region is short of GPUs.

choices.text: Reduce the job to a single node and accept that training takes roughly four times longer
choices.rationale: This changes the training design to dodge a capacity problem and still needs one A100 to be available on demand.

choices.text: Wrap job submission in a retry loop that resubmits every few minutes until capacity appears
choices.rationale: A retry loop competes for capacity blindly, gives no all-nodes-at-once start guarantee and adds failure handling you would have to maintain.

prompt: Cymbal's virtual shopping agent must answer questions about current product details and return policies, and Cymbal wants every answer tied to its own catalog and policy documents so it can be traced to sources. Which technique on the Agent Platform addresses this directly?

choices.text: Ground the model with Google Search so answers reflect public pages about similar products
choices.rationale: Google Search grounding draws on the public web, not Cymbal's private catalog or return policy.

choices.text: Ground the model with Agent Search or RAG Engine over the catalog and policy documents
choices.rationale: Grounding ties model output to verifiable data sources, reduces invented content and provides links to the supporting sources.

choices.text: Lower the model's temperature so that its replies invent fewer catalog details
choices.rationale: A lower temperature reduces randomness only. It does not connect answers to Cymbal's catalog and policy documents, and it provides no source links for traceability.

choices.text: Fine-tune the model on the current catalog again whenever a price or policy changes
choices.rationale: Repeated tuning is slow and costly for fast-changing facts, and it offers no source links for traceability.

prompt: Cymbal launches AI Commerce Search on its product pages. The first A/B test shows no lift in conversion over the existing search, and the merchandising team proposes adding dozens of boost and bury rules. What should the architect have the team check first?

choices.text: Cache each shopper's personalized results at the CDN to cut latency before the next test
choices.rationale: The documentation warns never to cache personalized results or return them to a different user.

choices.text: Replace the service with a custom ranking model trained on the very same events and catalog data
choices.rationale: That repeats the problem with more effort. If the underlying catalog and event data are flawed, a custom model inherits the flaws.

choices.text: Review catalog and user-event ingestion with the data quality dashboards, since relevance depends on that data
choices.rationale: Performance of AI Commerce Search is very sensitive to catalog and user-event data, and flawed data is more often the root cause of a flat A/B result than the service itself.

choices.text: Add the proposed rules now and rerun the test, since manual rules are how the service reaches parity
choices.rationale: Business rules should be applied only for specific, data-backed reasons. The goal is to let the AI ranking do its job, and new rules should be A/B tested.

prompt: Altostrat's metadata pipeline calls the Video Intelligence API to flag explicit content in video. Leadership also wants concise summaries of videos and podcasts, richer metadata and an auditable explanation for each flag, all over media already in Cloud Storage. The Video Intelligence API is now deprecated, with shutdown in September 2027. What should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Run Cloud Vision SafeSearch on extracted frames and skip the audio, summaries and extra metadata
choices.rationale: SafeSearch scores images only. It drops audio and does not produce summaries or reasoning.

choices.text: Train a custom video classifier for flags plus a separate model for each other required output
choices.rationale: This is a large build-and-maintain effort for tasks that prebuilt multimodal models already cover.

choices.text: Keep the Video Intelligence API for flags until shutdown and add a transcription workflow for summaries
choices.rationale: This leaves a deprecated dependency to migrate later and still yields no explanation for each flag.

choices.text: Move to Gemini multimodal models on the Agent Platform and prompt for summaries, metadata and reasoned flags
choices.rationale: Google recommends migrating from the deprecated API to Gemini models. One multimodal model can handle video and audio and return summaries, metadata and reasoned flags for review.

prompt: A health insurer wants a grounded assistant over 30,000 policy documents in PDF, DOCX and PPTX files that contain tables and lists. Retrieval quality has been poor because naive splitting breaks tables across chunks. Which two components should the architect use? (Choose two.)

choices.text: RAG Engine on the Agent Platform, to index the chunks and supply retrieved context to Gemini
choices.rationale: RAG Engine handles ingestion, indexing into a corpus, retrieval and generation, which grounds answers in the insurer's documents.

choices.text: Fine-tune Gemini on all 30,000 documents so that no retrieval layer is needed at all
choices.rationale: Tuning bakes in static knowledge and gives no source traceability. Policy content changes, which retrieval handles better.

choices.text: Document AI Layout Parser, to extract text, tables and lists and create context-aware chunks
choices.rationale: Layout Parser supports PDF, DOCX and PPTX and produces context-aware chunks meant for retrieval in generative AI applications.

choices.text: Document AI Form Parser, which creates context-aware chunks that suit retrieval over such documents
choices.rationale: Form Parser extracts key-value pairs, checkboxes and tables. Chunking for retrieval is the Layout Parser's job.

choices.text: A Document AI Custom Classifier, to generate the embeddings used for similarity search
choices.rationale: A classifier assigns documents to classes. It does not generate embeddings or retrieve passages.

prompt: Altostrat Media's legacy ingestion systems sit in a regional data center that is not in any Dedicated Interconnect colocation facility. Nightly ingestion of new footage needs about 8 Gbps sustained, traffic must reach private VPC addresses without crossing the public internet, and the ingestion path has a 99.99% availability target. Which connectivity design should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Partner Interconnect with redundant VLAN attachments in two metros and Cloud Routers exchanging routes over BGP
choices.rationale: Partner Interconnect is built for sites that cannot reach a Dedicated Interconnect colocation facility, reaches internal VPC addresses without the public internet, and supports 99.99% designs with redundant attachments across two metros.

choices.text: HA VPN with two tunnels to the on-premises gateway, since it carries a 99.99% SLA and needs no service provider or colocation
choices.rationale: HA VPN can reach the 99.99% SLA, but each tunnel is limited to roughly 1-3 Gbps and traffic from the data center crosses the public internet, so the sustained throughput and no-internet requirements fail.

choices.text: Dedicated Interconnect with four connections in two metros, ordered from Google and cross-connected to the data center
choices.rationale: Dedicated Interconnect requires the customer network to reach a colocation facility where Google is present. The stem says this data center cannot, so the physical connection cannot be built.

choices.text: Direct Peering at a nearby Google edge location, with BGP sessions to Google's edge network for private access
choices.rationale: Direct Peering is meant for Google Workspace and Google APIs, offers no SLA, and does not provide access to resources that have only internal IP addresses in a VPC.

explanation: Choose the hybrid link by what the site can physically reach, the bandwidth needed, and whether traffic may cross the internet: HA VPN for modest bandwidth, Partner Interconnect without colocation access, Dedicated Interconnect with it.

prompt: Altostrat Media wants two generative AI features built on its library in Cloud Storage: concise summaries of newly uploaded podcasts and interviews, and a discovery assistant that recommends only titles currently in the catalog, which changes daily as titles are added and withdrawn. The team has no labeled training data and little ML operations capacity. Which two approaches should the architect combine? Choose two.

choices.text: Prompt a Gemini model with each new audio or video file from Cloud Storage plus a summarization instruction
choices.rationale: Gemini accepts audio and video input from Cloud Storage and can summarize it. Prompting needs no labeled data and is the recommended starting point before any tuning.

choices.text: Ground the assistant with RAG Engine, ingesting catalog data from Cloud Storage and refreshing the corpus as titles change
choices.rationale: RAG retrieves current catalog content at request time, which reduces hallucinations and works around the model's knowledge cutoff, and RAG Engine can ingest data from Cloud Storage.

choices.text: Run supervised tuning of a Gemini model on the full transcript archive so that the model learns the whole catalog
choices.rationale: Tuning needs a sizable labeled dataset and is meant to fix recurring errors or style after prompting falls short. Catalog knowledge baked into weights goes stale when titles are withdrawn.

choices.text: Train a custom summarization model from scratch on the audio archive using custom training jobs on GPUs
choices.rationale: A from-scratch model needs labeled data and heavy ML operations, which the team lacks, and a foundation model already summarizes audio and video through prompting.

choices.text: Let Gemini answer recommendation questions from its pretrained knowledge, with an instruction to name only real Altostrat titles
choices.rationale: An instruction cannot supply a catalog the model never saw. Without retrieval the assistant will invent titles or recommend withdrawn ones.

explanation: Match the technique to the need: prompt a multimodal model for transformation tasks such as summarization, and ground it with retrieval when answers must reflect changing private data. Tune only when prompting falls short.

prompt: Cymbal receives supplier rows that each hold a product title, a free-text description and a photo. For every row it needs (1) attributes in the catalog's fixed structure, with values drawn from a controlled vocabulary per product category, and (2) color variants and background changes generated from the supplier's base photo. Both outputs go to an associate review UI. Which design on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform fits both needs?

choices.text: Prompt Gemini with the supplier data and set only the JSON response type, describing the attribute structure in the prompt, then edit the base photo with a Gemini image model.
choices.rationale: Setting the JSON response type without a response schema is only a strong hint and does not ensure valid JSON. Downstream review and catalog writes would break on malformed or off-vocabulary output.

choices.text: Prompt Gemini with the supplier data under a response schema that uses enum fields, then generate each variant from a text-only description of the product.
choices.rationale: The attribute half is correct, but a text-only description cannot reproduce the product shown in the supplier's photo, so the variants would not be derived from the base image as required.

choices.text: Prompt Gemini with the supplier title, description and photo under a response schema that uses enum fields, then prompt a Gemini image model to edit the base photo.
choices.rationale: A response schema makes the output follow the defined structure, and enum fields limit values to the controlled vocabulary. Gemini image models edit a supplied image from a natural-language prompt, with no mask needed.

choices.text: Train a custom image classifier for each attribute on past catalog photos, then script hue shifts over each base photo to produce the color variants.
choices.rationale: This needs per-attribute training data and ignores the title and description. Scripted hue shifts also cannot change backgrounds or add text overlays, which prompt-driven image editing can.

explanation: Constrain attribute generation with a response schema (enums for controlled values) and use prompt-driven Gemini image editing on the supplier's base photo, keeping an associate in the loop before the catalog updates.

prompt: EHR Healthcare serves its patient portal from GKE in a single region. Clinicians in Europe and Asia report slow page loads, and profiling shows most of the delay is spent downloading JavaScript bundles and images that are stored in a Cloud Storage bucket. Patient record API responses are personalized and contain PHI. The goal is to reduce latency for all customers without caching PHI at the edge. Which design meets this goal?

choices.text: Create a regional external Application Load Balancer in each continent behind DNS round-robin and enable Cloud CDN on each of them
choices.rationale: Cloud CDN works with the global external or classic Application Load Balancer, so regional load balancers cannot provide it. Round-robin DNS also does not steer users to their nearest region.

choices.text: Enable Cloud CDN on every backend and use the force-cache-all mode so that even API responses come from edge caches near users
choices.rationale: Force-cache-all ignores private and no-store directives and can cache per-user, identifiable content. Google advises it only for backends such as Cloud Storage buckets, never for personalized API responses.

choices.text: Use a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN on the static-asset bucket, leaving the API backend uncached
choices.rationale: Cloud CDN serves cacheable static content from edge locations close to users through a global external Application Load Balancer, and leaving the API backend without caching keeps per-user PHI out of the edge caches.

choices.text: Add GKE nodes and Pod replicas in the current region so that each request is processed faster before it travels to the user
choices.rationale: More capacity shortens processing time but not the distance each asset travels. Profiling shows download time, not server processing, is the delay, so scaling the origin leaves distant users slow.

explanation: Put the edge cache where content is static and shared, and keep it away from personalized responses. Cloud CDN's cache mode decides what is stored, so avoid forcing everything into the cache on mixed backends.

prompt: KnightMotives Automotive stores crash-test sensor recordings from its autonomous-driving programme in a Cloud Storage bucket. Safety regulators require every recording to be kept for at least ten years, and counsel wants a guarantee that nobody, including project owners, can delete or overwrite a recording before then. Which configuration meets the requirement?

choices.text: Set a ten-year retention policy on the bucket and lock it, so objects cannot be deleted or replaced until they reach that age
choices.rationale: A locked retention policy is irreversible: it cannot be removed or shortened, and an object cannot be deleted or overwritten until it has met the retention period. The bucket itself cannot be deleted until every object has met it.

choices.text: Turn on Object Versioning, so that every deleted or overwritten recording stays in the bucket as a noncurrent version for years
choices.rationale: Versioning keeps earlier versions but enforces no minimum age: anyone holding delete permission can still remove noncurrent versions. Only a retention policy blocks deletion until an object reaches a given age.

choices.text: Raise the soft delete retention window to its maximum, so any deleted recording can be restored for as long as needed
choices.rationale: Soft delete retention can be set only between 7 and 90 days, far short of ten years, and it is a recovery window for deleted objects rather than a control that blocks deletion.

choices.text: Set a ten-year retention policy but leave it unlocked, so the team can adjust the period if the regulation changes
choices.rationale: Unless a retention policy is locked, it can be increased, decreased or removed. An administrator could shorten it and then delete recordings early, which is exactly what counsel wants to rule out.

explanation: Only a locked retention policy makes deletion before a set age impossible for every principal; versioning and soft delete aid recovery, and an unlocked policy can still be changed.

prompt: KnightMotives serves a tabular gradient-boosted model from a Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform online endpoint. It suggests in-vehicle climate and navigation settings for each driver. After a launch in Nordic markets, engineers worry that winter driving patterns differ from the training data, but drivers' accept-or-reject outcomes are only joined back to the requests about six weeks later. The original training table is in BigQuery. The team wants an early warning that needs no labels, delivered to the ML on-call channel. What should they do?

choices.text: Enable Model Monitoring on the endpoint, with skew detection against the BigQuery training table and alerts sent to a notification channel
choices.rationale: Model Monitoring logs online requests and compares the distribution of each input feature with the training data, so no outcome labels are needed. It alerts by email or through Cloud Monitoring channels when a feature passes its threshold, and it supports tabular models like this one.

choices.text: Create Cloud Monitoring alerting policies on the endpoint's latency, error rate and CPU utilization, and page the on-call when any of them is breached
choices.rationale: Those metrics describe serving health. An endpoint can answer quickly and without errors while receiving inputs that look nothing like the training data, so they cannot reveal a changed feature distribution.

choices.text: Run scheduled model evaluations against ground-truth outcomes and alert the on-call when accuracy falls below the agreed target
choices.rationale: Evaluation compares predictions with real outcomes, and those arrive about six weeks late. The warning would come after drivers had already received weeks of poor suggestions, whereas input monitoring needs no labels.

choices.text: Retrain the model every night in a pipeline on the newest logged requests, so it adapts to winter without any monitoring in place
choices.rationale: The newest requests have no outcome labels yet, so there is nothing valid to train on. Retraining blindly also gives the team no signal about whether inputs shifted, which features moved, or when.

explanation: When labels lag, monitor the input distribution against the training baseline and alert on thresholds; evaluation and retraining come after that signal.

prompt: Altostrat Media wants 24/7 self-service support for subscribers with billing, playback and account questions. The answers live in a help-center website of several hundred HTML and PDF pages that change weekly, plus policy documents in Cloud Storage. Replies must link to the page they came from, and a subscriber who asks for a person must reach the human support team. The team has no NLU specialists and no labeled conversation data. What should the architect build?

choices.text: A Gemini model behind Cloud Run with the entire help-center text pasted into the system instruction and a custom handoff service
choices.rationale: The corpus is re-pasted on every request, goes stale with each weekly change, may not fit the context window, and yields no retrieval-based source links. The handoff would also be custom code.

choices.text: A flow-based Dialogflow CX agent where staff write an intent with training phrases and a fixed reply for each help topic
choices.rationale: This works for a short list of stable topics, but several hundred pages that change weekly would need constant manual authoring, and fixed replies give no generated, source-linked answers from the live content.

choices.text: A Conversational Agents agent with a data store over the help site and bucket, giving cited answers and human routing
choices.rationale: Data store handlers produce LLM answers grounded in the site and uploaded content, return the sources they used, and the agent routes requests such as talking to a human through generated intents. It needs no labeled data.

choices.text: Supervised tuning of a Gemini model on archived support chats so it memorizes policies, plus a custom handoff service for humans
choices.rationale: Tuning adjusts model behavior and style rather than serving as a store of changing facts, needs labeled examples the team lacks, and gives no source citations. Weekly policy changes would need repeated tuning.

explanation: For support answers drawn from changing documentation, ground a conversational agent in a data store rather than hand-authoring intents or baking content into prompts or weights. Note that the data stores feature is excluded from the Dialogflow CX SLA, so critical journeys may still warrant deterministic flows alongside it. Google is consolidating Dialogflow CX under the Conversational Agents name.

prompt: Altostrat Media is adding a personalized home-page row to its streaming site using a media recommendations app in Vertex AI Search (being renamed Agent Search). The app is configured with the Recommended for You type, the Home Page Context event type, and the watch duration per session objective. Months of events are already imported from BigQuery, yet the team cannot get a model trained for this configuration. The exhibit shows the event counts. What should the architect change?

exhibit.label: User events ingested into the app, last 90 days
exhibit.content:
Event type        | Events  | Unique user pseudo IDs
view-item         | 412,000 | 38,200
media-play        |  95,000 | 21,400
media-complete    |       0 |      0
view-home-page    |       0 |      0
search            |       0 |      0

choices.text: Import more historical view-item events from BigQuery until the volume clears the minimum needed to optimize recommendations
choices.rationale: Volume is not the gap. The 412,000 view-item events already exceed the documented 250,000 minimum, and more of the same event type cannot supply the missing completion and home-page events.

choices.text: Keep Home Page Context and switch the objective to click-through rate, which needs only the view-item events already ingested
choices.rationale: Click-through optimization would drop the media-complete need, but Home Page Context still requires view-home-page events, which the exhibit shows are absent, so this configuration still cannot train.

choices.text: Change the type to Most Popular, which ranks recently popular titles and needs no per-listener event types to be recorded
choices.rationale: Most Popular recommends what is popular across all users within a time window. It is not personalized to each listener, so it abandons the personalization goal instead of fixing the missing events.

choices.text: Record media-complete events with progress duration and view-home-page events with panel info from the player and home page
choices.rationale: The watch duration objective needs media-complete events alongside play or view events, and Home Page Context needs view-home-page events. Panel info also lets recommendations be attributed to specific home-page panels.

explanation: Match the app's type, context and objective to the event types actually instrumented. A diagnosis starts by comparing the required events for the chosen objective with what the exhibit shows has arrived.

prompt: Associates at Cymbal approve gen AI-generated titles, descriptions and brand values before the catalog is updated. The website, the mobile app and AI Commerce Search must all show the same approved text, and new supplier products should be searchable the day they are approved. The catalog changes constantly. How should approved content reach AI Commerce Search?

choices.text: Keep the catalog database as the source of truth and, after each approval, patch the changed products' built-in title, description and brand fields in AI Commerce Search.
choices.rationale: Patching updates only the changed fields, so approved content flows daily or faster. Built-in fields such as title, description and brand have a larger effect on searchability than custom attributes. The same source feeds every channel.

choices.text: Store each approved description as a custom attribute marked searchable and leave the built-in product fields as the supplier supplied them.
choices.rationale: Custom attributes can be made searchable, but built-in fields such as title, description and brands have a bigger impact on searchability and indexability. Leaving them as supplied wastes the enrichment.

choices.text: Re-import the full catalog from Cloud Storage once a week, together with the other channel feeds, so that all three channels change on the same schedule.
choices.rationale: Google recommends uploading catalog changes ideally every day when the catalog changes often. A weekly cycle delays searchability well beyond the same-day goal even though the channels stay aligned.

choices.text: Keep approved text only in the catalog database and feed search the original supplier text, since relevance is driven by user events and not by catalog fields.
choices.rationale: Search performance is sensitive to the uploaded catalog, product information and user events alike. Withholding the enriched fields leaves AI Commerce Search with weaker text and the channels inconsistent.

explanation: Treat the approved catalog record as the single source of truth and push changed fields incrementally to AI Commerce Search, using the built-in fields that matter most for search quality.

prompt: Every weekday at 08:00 clinics open and EHR Healthcare's patient-portal traffic rises about eightfold within three minutes. The portal runs on a GKE Standard cluster with a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on CPU and node pool autoscaling enabled. The exhibit shows what the on-call engineer captured during the last spike, when users received 503 errors. EHR wants the errors gone without paying for a full-size fleet all day and without hand-managed scheduled scaling. What should the architect change?

exhibit.label: Events during the 08:00 spike
exhibit.content:
08:00:40 HPA portal      cpu 187%/60%  replicas 8 -> 24  (maxReplicas 120)
08:00:42 Pod portal-7f9c-x4k2  Pending: 0/6 nodes are available: 6 Insufficient cpu
08:00:43 ClusterAutoscaler     TriggeredScaleUp: portal-pool 6 -> 14 nodes  (max 40)
08:00:45 Gateway               503 upstream_unavailable (16 replicas unschedulable)
08:02:58 Node portal-pool-n7   Ready (first added node)
08:03:10 Pod portal-7f9c-x4k2  Scheduled, Running
08:03:30 Gateway               503 rate back to baseline

choices.text: Raise the HPA maximum replica count well above 120 and lower the CPU target to 30% so that more replicas are created sooner
choices.rationale: The HPA is not capped: it asked for 24 of an allowed 120 and was acting immediately. More or earlier replicas would only create more Pending Pods, because the delay comes from waiting for nodes.

choices.text: Raise the node pool's autoscaling maximum from 40 nodes to 100 so that the cluster autoscaler can add more nodes during a spike
choices.rationale: The cluster autoscaler scaled up at once to 14 of a maximum of 40, so the limit was never reached. The errors lasted only for the roughly two minutes it took the first new node to become Ready.

choices.text: Add a Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode on the portal Deployment so that each Pod's CPU request grows as load increases
choices.rationale: Larger requests need even more node capacity and do not remove the wait for new nodes. Google advises against combining the vertical and horizontal autoscalers on the same CPU or memory metric.

choices.text: Deploy low-priority placeholder Pods that reserve spare node capacity, so that portal replicas preempt them and start without waiting for new nodes
choices.rationale: Placeholder Pods hold ready capacity at a lower priority. When the HPA adds portal replicas they evict the placeholders and schedule immediately, and the autoscaler then replaces the buffer. EHR chooses how big a buffer to pay for.

explanation: The exhibit shows both autoscalers working and no limit being hit: the outage window is node provisioning time. A reserved buffer of low-priority placeholder Pods trades a small standing cost for immediate scheduling.

prompt: KnightMotives is modernizing its legacy ICE models with a multi-gigabyte software package delivered over the air. Only entitled vehicles may download it, and an entitlement check runs in an update service. Most vehicles in a country fetch the same package within the same week, and many are on rural cellular links that drop mid-download, so the download must resume. Dealers have no budget for new equipment. Which delivery design fits best?

choices.text: Keep the package in a Cloud Storage backend bucket behind a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN, and issue short-lived signed URLs
choices.rationale: Cloud CDN can use a backend bucket as origin and serves repeated downloads from edge caches. Signed URLs grant time-limited access to anyone holding them, so the update service can gate entitlement, and byte range support lets interrupted downloads resume.

choices.text: Keep the package in a regional bucket and have the update service issue Cloud Storage signed URLs that vehicles use directly, with no load balancer or cache in front of the bucket
choices.rationale: Signed URLs do control access and ranged reads work, but every vehicle download is then served from the origin bucket's location. Repeated downloads of the same package gain no edge caching, so latency and origin load are worse than with Cloud CDN.

choices.text: Run a managed instance group that holds the package on persistent disks behind a regional load balancer, and have all vehicles download it from those VMs
choices.rationale: This can work, but capacity is sized for the peak week and the team patches and scales the servers. Cloud Storage with Cloud CDN is built for large static objects and absorbs the repeated downloads at the edge.

choices.text: Replicate the package to a file server at every dealership, and have vehicles update over the dealer network when parked on the lot
choices.rationale: Dealers have no budget for new equipment, and a fleet of servers to replicate and secure is a heavy burden. It also excludes owners who rarely visit a dealer, which are the rural vehicles with the worst connectivity.

explanation: For large, widely repeated downloads to unreliable clients, serve from Cloud Storage through a load balancer with Cloud CDN and gate access with short-lived signed URLs.

prompt: Redwood Mutual, an insurer, writes a nightly export of its claims database to a Cloud Storage bucket. A lifecycle rule deletes each export 400 days after creation. No restore has been needed in four years, but the disaster recovery plan says a full restore must begin reading data within one hour of a declaration. Which storage class is the best fit for the export bucket?

choices.text: Coldline, because Archive objects take hours to restore and so could not meet a one-hour deadline to begin reading the data.
choices.rationale: This treats Archive like tape or a deep-archive tier. In Cloud Storage, Archive data is available within milliseconds, so the recovery window is not a reason to pay Coldline storage rates for data this cold.

choices.text: Nearline, because any colder class would add early deletion charges to exports that the lifecycle rule removes after 400 days.
choices.rationale: The early deletion charge applies only to objects deleted or replaced before the minimum duration. Archive's minimum is 365 days, which these objects exceed, so Nearline's higher at-rest cost buys nothing here.

choices.text: Archive, because the exports outlive its minimum duration and a rare restore justifies paying retrieval fees for millisecond access.
choices.rationale: Archive is meant for data read less than once a year. Its minimum duration is 365 days, so deleting at 400 days triggers no early deletion charge, and it serves reads with low latency, so a restore can begin within the hour.

choices.text: Standard, because it is the only class with no retrieval fees, and the restore has to begin reading data within the hour.
choices.rationale: Standard does have no retrieval fee, but its at-rest cost is the highest. Data read less than once a year is the pattern retrieval-fee classes are priced for, and a restore that may never happen does not justify Standard rates.

explanation: Cloud Storage classes trade at-rest price against retrieval fees and a minimum storage duration (Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90, Archive 365). All of them, Archive included, return data with low latency. Pick the coldest class whose minimum duration the data's real lifetime exceeds and whose access frequency matches.

prompt: Northwind Vision trains an image model on 300 TB of data held in a Cloud Storage bucket, using 128 GPUs across many nodes in one zone. Every node must read the same dataset in parallel and write synchronous checkpoints through standard POSIX file operations. The company wants the bucket to stay the durable system of record. Which design fits?

choices.text: Create a Managed Lustre instance, import the dataset, and delete the bucket copy so that Lustre becomes the only system of record.
choices.rationale: Managed Lustre is persistent, but Google's guidance is to treat it as working storage and keep data and checkpoints in Cloud Storage. Deleting the bucket copy removes the durable repository the company wants to keep.

choices.text: Create a Managed Lustre instance in the GPU zone, import the dataset, checkpoint to it, and export checkpoints to the bucket.
choices.rationale: Managed Lustre is a POSIX parallel file system with sub-millisecond latency, recommended for training and checkpointing when clients sit in the same zone. Cloud Storage stays the central repository through import and export.

choices.text: Copy the dataset to Local SSD on each GPU node, checkpoint there, and synchronize the files between nodes on a schedule.
choices.rationale: Local SSD is attached to a single host, and its data may be lost whenever the VM stops or is terminated. It is not a shared file system, so it cannot hold the checkpoints or give all nodes one view of the data.

choices.text: Mount the bucket on every node with Cloud Storage FUSE and Rapid Cache, and use that mount for all reads and synchronous checkpoints.
choices.rationale: FUSE with Rapid Cache is the recommended choice for serving and inference, where lower cost matters. It is an adapter, not a native POSIX file system, and it offers lower per-VM throughput than Managed Lustre.

explanation: For multi-node training that needs POSIX semantics and low latency, Managed Lustre in the compute zone is the working store, with Cloud Storage as the durable repository. Cloud Storage FUSE with Rapid Cache is the recommended pairing for serving and inference.

prompt: A fintech's security policy forbids external IP addresses on Compute Engine VMs, and the company has no VPN. Administrators on corporate laptops must still reach SSH on private VMs in a custom-mode VPC, with each access decision made per user through IAM. Which two actions meet these requirements? Choose two.

choices.text: Grant the administrators the IAP-secured Tunnel User role on the project or on the target VMs.
choices.rationale: IAP TCP forwarding authorizes each user through IAM, and this role is what permits a user to open a tunnel to a VM. No external IP is needed on the VM.

choices.text: Add an ingress firewall rule allowing TCP port 22 from 35.235.240.0/20, the range IAP uses for TCP forwarding.
choices.rationale: Tunneled connections reach the VM from that Google-owned range. Without this ingress rule the VPC drops them, because a custom-mode VPC denies ingress by default.

choices.text: Create a Cloud NAT gateway on the subnet so that administrators can open SSH sessions through the NAT address.
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT translates outbound connections from VMs without external IPs and passes only replies to them. It does not allow unsolicited inbound connections such as a new SSH session.

choices.text: Enable Private Google Access on the subnet so that laptops can reach the VMs' SSH port over Google's network.
choices.rationale: Private Google Access lets VMs with internal IPs initiate connections to Google APIs and services. It is an outbound mechanism and gives no inbound path from administrators' laptops.

choices.text: Deploy a bastion VM with an external IP and allow SSH to it from the corporate egress range.
choices.rationale: A bastion can work in general, but here it needs an external IP, which the policy forbids. It also adds a host to patch and does not make the per-user IAM access decision.

explanation: IAP TCP forwarding needs two things: an IAM grant that lets the user tunnel, and a firewall rule that lets IAP's range reach the port. Nothing needs an external IP or a VPN.

prompt: A team is moving a per-vCPU-licensed database to a Compute Engine VM. The sizing profile is shown. Which machine configuration meets the need while keeping the licensed vCPU count as low as possible?

exhibit.label: Sizing profile and licence terms
exhibit.content:
Item | Value
Database licence | Charged for every vCPU of the VM
Measured need | 6 vCPUs and 42 GB of memory
Platform standard | General-purpose N-series; no extended memory

choices.text: A custom machine type on the N2D series with exactly 6 vCPUs and 42 GB of memory.
choices.rationale: N2D custom accepts only specific vCPU counts: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80 or 96. Six is not allowed, so the configuration cannot be created.

choices.text: The predefined n2-highmem-8 type (8 vCPUs, 64 GB), the nearest shape that covers the memory.
choices.rationale: It covers the memory, but it brings two extra vCPUs. The licence charges for every vCPU, so this over-licenses the database. Custom machine types exist to avoid this.

choices.text: A custom machine type on the N2 series with exactly 6 vCPUs and 42 GB of memory.
choices.rationale: N2 custom accepts 6 vCPUs, and 42 GB is 7 GB per vCPU, inside the default per-vCPU memory range. Custom sizing avoids paying for licensed vCPUs the workload does not use.

choices.text: A custom machine type on the N1 series with exactly 6 vCPUs and 42 GB of memory.
choices.rationale: N1 custom allows up to 6.5 GB per vCPU, which is 39 GB at 6 vCPUs. The 42 GB request would need extended memory, which the platform standard excludes.

explanation: Custom machine types let you pick the vCPU count and memory within per-series limits, which matters most with per-vCPU licensing. Check the series' allowed vCPU counts and its memory-per-vCPU ceiling before choosing one. Extended memory goes beyond that ceiling at a premium.

prompt: Helix Genomics will fine-tune a protein model starting in 45 days on 64 GPU VMs that must sit together in one tightly coupled cluster. The run needs about 21 days of continuous, uninterrupted capacity, GPU capacity in the target zone is scarce, and the team wants to pay only for those 21 days. Which approach should the architect choose?

choices.text: Create an on-demand reservation for the 64 GPU VMs today, so capacity is held until the run begins, and delete it afterwards
choices.rationale: An on-demand reservation is billed at the on-demand rate from the moment it exists, used or not. Holding it for 45 idle days before the run breaks the requirement to pay only for the 21 days of work.

choices.text: Buy a three-year resource-based committed use discount for the GPU VMs, which secures the capacity and lowers the price of the run
choices.rationale: A resource-based commitment is a billing discount, not a capacity guarantee; capacity needs a reservation. It also cannot be canceled, so the team would pay for three years to cover a 21-day job.

choices.text: Request a calendar-mode future reservation of 64 GPU VMs for a 21-day period, then launch reservation-bound VMs at its start
choices.rationale: Calendar mode reserves GPU capacity for a fixed period of 24 hours to 90 days. GPU requests open up to 60 days ahead, so 45 days is in range, and allocation is dense for cluster training. Billing starts when the request is fulfilled.

choices.text: Submit a Flex-start VM request for 64 GPU VMs and let Dynamic Workload Scheduler provision them together once capacity frees up
choices.rationale: Flex-start VMs run for at most seven days and are provisioned on a best-effort basis when resources are available. A 21-day run exceeds that limit and there is no assurance the capacity arrives by the start date.

choices.text: Run the job on Spot VMs, which give the deepest discount, and rely on frequent checkpoints to recover when instances are reclaimed
choices.rationale: Spot VMs can be stopped or deleted at any time to reclaim capacity and carry no capacity assurance. The run requires uninterrupted capacity in a scarce zone, so a discount cannot make up for the missing guarantee.

explanation: Match the capacity tool to the duration and start date. Calendar-mode future reservations cover GPU, H4D or TPU capacity for up to 90 days at a known future start. Standard future reservations take start dates up to one year out with no stated maximum length, but Google recommends periods of 365 days or longer to improve approval odds and GPU requests need the account team. Flex-start is best-effort and capped at seven days. Committed use discounts cut price but never reserve capacity.

prompt: Ferrous Ridge, a steel fabricator, has 14,000 photos of weld seams. Inspectors labeled each photo with one of nine company-specific defect classes. The company has two quality engineers and no ML engineers. It wants a trained model that it can evaluate against held-out labeled photos and deploy to an endpoint with as little code as possible. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Call Cloud Vision API label detection on each photo and map the returned labels onto the nine defect classes with rules
choices.rationale: Label detection returns general labels from Google's predefined categories. It knows nothing about the company's nine weld-defect classes, and the 14,000 labeled photos would go unused.

choices.text: Prompt Gemini on every request with the nine class definitions and a few sample photos, and skip training altogether
choices.rationale: Prompting a foundation model does not learn from the 14,000 labeled photos and gives no held-out evaluation of a model the company owns. Prompting suits tasks without labeled data; here the labels are the asset.

choices.text: Train an AutoML image classifier on the labeled photos, review its evaluation metrics, then deploy it to an endpoint
choices.rationale: AutoML lets a team create and train a model with minimal technical effort and no programming. It fits a standard objective such as image classification with the team's own labeled data.

choices.text: Write a training application around a custom CNN and run it as a custom training job on Agent Platform with GPUs
choices.rationale: Custom training gives full control over architecture and loss, but it needs data science and programming skills the team lacks. Reserve it for cases where AutoML cannot meet the need, which a standard classification task does not show.

explanation: Choose the lightest approach that uses the data you have. Pretrained APIs cover common tasks with no training data, prompting or tuning a foundation model suits language and multimodal generation, AutoML trains standard objectives on your labeled data with no code, and custom training is for architectures or loss functions AutoML cannot express.

prompt: Marlowe Outfitters, an online retailer with 2 million SKUs, wants storefront search and browse that tolerate misspellings, offer facets, and rank results by what shoppers actually click and buy. It has 18 months of storefront clickstream, a product catalog in BigQuery, and three engineers but no ML staff. Launch is next quarter. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Use AI Commerce Search (formerly Vertex AI Search for commerce): import the catalog and user events and let it rank results
choices.rationale: The retail-specific service takes a product catalog and user events, and handles data preprocessing, model training, hyperparameter tuning and serving. It provides search, browse and recommendations without an ML team.

choices.text: Create an Agent Search app over a website data store that crawls the storefront's product pages and enable its standard search features
choices.rationale: A generic app indexes page content. It is not the commerce product that ingests a structured catalog plus shopper events to rank by purchase behavior, which is the requirement.

choices.text: Train a two-tower ranking model on the clickstream with custom training, then serve candidates from Vector Search behind a custom API
choices.rationale: This can work, but it recreates what the managed service already handles. Three engineers with no ML staff would spend the quarter on data pipelines, training and serving instead of launching.

choices.text: Load the whole product catalog into Gemini's context with each query and ask the model to return the best-matching products
choices.rationale: Two million products are far more catalog data than fits in a prompt. Even a subset would add cost and latency to every query, and the model would not learn from the clickstream the retailer already holds.

explanation: For retail product discovery, AI Commerce Search (formerly Vertex AI Search for commerce, earlier Retail API) is the purpose-built managed option. Its inputs are the product catalog and user events, and the same data feeds search, browse and recommendations.

prompt: Linden Freight uploads scanned manifests to a Cloud Storage bucket in me-west1. An Eventarc trigger in me-west1 filters on google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized and targets the manifest-api Cloud Run service. The security team forbids allUsers on that service. The trigger was created with --service-account=manifest-trigger@ and shows no error, but the service never receives events. The exhibit lists the relevant IAM bindings. What should the architect change?

exhibit.label: IAM bindings relevant to the trigger
exhibit.content:
Principal                              | Role                      | Granted on
manifest-trigger@ (trigger identity)   | roles/eventarc.eventReceiver | project
manifest-runtime@ (service identity)   | roles/run.invoker         | service manifest-api
Cloud Storage service agent            | roles/pubsub.publisher    | project

choices.text: Grant roles/run.invoker on the manifest-api service to the trigger's service account, since that identity makes the authenticated call
choices.rationale: The trigger uses its service account as its identity when it calls the service, and that account needs the Cloud Run invoker role. The exhibit grants invoker to the runtime identity, which does not call the service.

choices.text: Grant roles/eventarc.eventReceiver to the runtime service account as well, so the service is allowed to receive the forwarded events
choices.rationale: The event receiver role belongs to the trigger's identity, which already has it. The runtime identity is what the service runs as; it never receives events on its own behalf.

choices.text: Add allUsers as an invoker of the service, so the trigger's delivery requests are accepted without needing authentication
choices.rationale: This would likely make deliveries work, but it opens the service to the internet and breaks the stated security rule. The least-privilege fix is to grant invoker to the trigger's identity alone.

choices.text: Grant roles/pubsub.publisher to the trigger's service account, because Eventarc moves the object events through Pub/Sub
choices.rationale: Publisher access is needed by the Cloud Storage service agent, which already has it in the exhibit. The trigger identity receives and delivers events and does not publish them.

explanation: For a Cloud Storage trigger to Cloud Run, three identities matter. The Cloud Storage service agent needs pubsub.publisher, the trigger's service account needs eventarc.eventReceiver and run.invoker, and the runtime identity is unrelated to delivery. Compare each binding with the identity that performs the action.

prompt: Kedem Insurance serves policyholders only in Israel and has a single Google Cloud region there, me-west1. Its regulator requires that client TLS sessions terminate inside the country. The team also wants URL-based HTTP(S) routing and managed certificates. Which design meets the mandate?

choices.text: A global external Application Load Balancer with every backend instance group placed in me-west1
choices.rationale: Global load balancers terminate TLS at locations distributed worldwide, so placing all backends in one region does not confine where client handshakes end.

choices.text: A regional external Application Load Balancer deployed in me-west1, with backends in the same region
choices.rationale: A regional external Application Load Balancer is the documented way to guarantee that TLS terminates only in the region where it is deployed, while still giving URL maps and certificates.

choices.text: A global external Application Load Balancer protected by a Cloud Armor policy that allows only Israeli IP ranges
choices.rationale: Cloud Armor geo and IP rules filter which requests are admitted. They do not change where the load balancer terminates the connection.

choices.text: A global external Application Load Balancer, with the resource locations organization policy limited to me-west1
choices.rationale: The resource locations constraint controls only where resources are created. It is not a statement about where a global load balancer terminates client connections.

explanation: When a mandate is about where the TLS handshake ends, load balancer scope decides the answer. Backend location, edge filtering and resource-creation policies do not.

prompt: Almog Health serves patients across the EU and must keep patient records stored and processed on infrastructure located in the EU. Its regulator's written guidance covers where data is stored and where application code runs, and says nothing about where encrypted client connections end. Almog wants one anycast IP, Cloud CDN for static assets and automatic failover between europe-west1 and europe-west4. Which design fits?

choices.text: A regional external Application Load Balancer in each EU region, with DNS records Almog manages to steer clients
choices.rationale: This solves a termination-location rule that the regulator never wrote, and it gives up the single anycast IP, Cloud CDN and automatic failover Almog asked for.

choices.text: One regional external Application Load Balancer in europe-west4 with backends in both europe-west1 and europe-west4
choices.rationale: A regional load balancer connects only to backends in its own region, so it cannot front both EU regions and fail over between them.

choices.text: A global external Application Load Balancer with backends only in europe-west1 and europe-west4, plus EU data stores
choices.rationale: Storage and processing stay in the EU through the backends and data stores, and the global scope supplies the anycast IP, Cloud CDN and cross-region failover the stem asks for.

choices.text: A global external Application Load Balancer on Standard Network Service Tier, so that all traffic stays inside the EU
choices.rationale: Global external Application Load Balancers run on Premium Tier only, and the network tier is not a data-residency control.

explanation: Regional is not automatically right for residency. It is right when the rule is about TLS termination location. Here the rule covers storage and processing, which the backends and data stores satisfy.

prompt: Kedem's regulated claims portal runs behind a regional external Application Load Balancer in me-west1, chosen so that TLS terminates in the country. The reliability lead now asks for a single IP address that automatically fails over to europe-west1 if me-west1 is lost. The compliance officer confirms that the in-country termination mandate has no exception for outages. What should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Add europe-west1 instance groups as extra backends of the same regional load balancer, so it can fail over when needed
choices.rationale: A regional load balancer can connect only to backends in its own region, so this configuration is not available.

choices.text: Replace it with a global external Application Load Balancer and add Cloud Armor geo rules that favor Israeli clients
choices.rationale: The global load balancer terminates TLS at locations distributed worldwide, and geo rules do not move the handshake, so the mandate is broken.

choices.text: Publish a DNS failover record that sends clients to a second regional load balancer in europe-west1 when health checks fail
choices.rationale: This does provide cross-region failover, but clients would then terminate TLS in Belgium, which is exactly what the mandate forbids.

choices.text: Keep the regional load balancer, use every zone of me-west1, and explain that failing over abroad would break the mandate
choices.rationale: Zonal resilience inside the region respects the mandate. A single-IP regional failover to another country is not possible, and moving traffic abroad would end TLS outside the territory.

explanation: The regional load balancer trades away the global VIP and cross-region failover. When the mandate has no outage exception, that trade-off is intentional, and the answer is resilience inside the territory.

prompt: Tallis Auctions runs a live bidding room as a Cloud Run service over WebSockets. Room membership and the current top bid are held in instance memory, session affinity is enabled and minimum instances is set to 3. During scale-in and new revisions, bidders report dropped connections and rooms that reset to an empty state. Which two changes fix the root cause? Choose two.

choices.text: Keep room state in Memorystore for Redis and use Redis Pub/Sub to coordinate updates between instances
choices.rationale: Instances are disposable, so room state must live outside them. Redis Pub/Sub also lets every instance see updates made on any other instance.

choices.text: Raise minimum instances so that the instances holding live rooms are never shut down or replaced during scale-in
choices.rationale: Minimum instances reduce cold starts. Cloud Run can still shut down and replace any instance, including those it keeps warm.

choices.text: Make the client library reconnect automatically after a drop and resume the room from the stored state
choices.rationale: Connections end at the timeout and when instances are replaced, so clients must reconnect and rebuild their view from external state.

choices.text: Raise maximum concurrency so that every bidder of a room lands on the same instance through session affinity
choices.rationale: Session affinity is best effort and breaks when an instance terminates or reaches its limits, so it cannot be the only place room state lives.

explanation: WebSockets are supported on Cloud Run, but instances are replaceable and affinity is best effort. The durable design externalizes state and reconnects clients.

prompt: Brightwave Games is moving multiplayer game servers to Google Cloud. Game clients exchange custom binary packets over UDP, the server must see each player's real source IP for anti-cheat checks, and a small operations team scales the fleet by region. A developer proposes Cloud Run because the team prefers serverless. Which platform meets the protocol requirement?

choices.text: A Cloud Run service with WebSockets enabled, behind a global external Application Load Balancer using a serverless NEG
choices.rationale: Cloud Run services and Application Load Balancers handle HTTP-family traffic. Raw UDP from game clients cannot be carried over them.

choices.text: A Cloud Run worker pool with instance-based billing and minimum instances, scaled manually in each region
choices.rationale: Worker pools run pull-based background work and do not expose a public endpoint for client packets, so they are not a UDP front end.

choices.text: Compute Engine instances in a managed instance group behind a regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer
choices.rationale: A passthrough Network Load Balancer carries UDP and delivers packets with the client source IP unchanged to instance-group backends.

choices.text: GKE Autopilot Pods published through the Gateway API, with an HTTPRoute defined for each game server
choices.rationale: Gateway API HTTPRoutes provision HTTP(S) routing, not UDP passthrough, so game packets would not reach the Pods.

explanation: Serverless is the reflex here, but the protocol decides. Raw TCP or UDP workloads belong on Compute Engine or GKE behind a passthrough Network Load Balancer.

prompt: A collaborative whiteboard on Cloud Run keeps each user's WebSocket open for sessions that often last three hours. The team sets the request timeout to its maximum and expects every connection to survive the whole session. What must the design still include?

choices.text: Nothing more, because the maximum timeout setting is large enough to cover three-hour sessions once WebSockets are enabled
